name: Priya Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; this is confidential, and your name won't go in our findings. What does a usual day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Priya, 43, a junior lineworker. I pick up the paper switching order at the depot, check the insulated gloves and grounding rods, then ride with the crew to inspect or repair a power line. I keep the order in a clear sleeve so it doesn't turn to pulp in the rain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work do you enjoy, and what is hardest to carry home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when the switching order makes sense at the pole and the crew can finish without rushing. The wind makes everything harder, and after a long shift I still have a mortgage and two children, ages 7 and 14, to keep on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like a few easier forms at the depot and the same work in the rain. I would still check the written switching order against the pole number before the crew starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paper log catches what the screen misses when the road sign is wrong. I'd say a small time saving is welcome, but it doesn't replace walking the site and reading the pole marker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think this mild version takes my job, because I'm mostly outside with the crew. My pay is low and our savings are less than a month of bills, so the mortgage already takes more thought than a new form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking the lead to check me on the written switching order until I can catch a mismatch myself. I would leave the household budget as it is and avoid buying a new appliance unless the old one failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm steady about the work, but anxious about money even in this quiet picture. The mortgage, school shoes, and fuel still arrive whether AI changes anything or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the switching order do you double-check most often?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the pole number and the feeder name, because a neat sheet can still have the wrong location. I ask the crew lead to confirm if anything doesn't match the marker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the new form showed a detail you couldn't verify in the field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop and ask the lead to call the dispatcher before the crew moved on. I don't want a faster form to make us skip a check we already know how to do.

say: I say **my paper log** catches errors when a road sign is wrong.
I welcome small savings, but I still want a person to **walk the site**.
think: I don't expect this mild version to take my **field job**.
I still worry about **mortgage and school costs** because savings cover less than a month.
do: Keep checking the **switching order** with the crew lead.
Avoid replacing an appliance unless the **old one fails**.
feel: I'm steady about work, but **household money** keeps me anxious.
S0.quote: My paper log catches what the screen misses when the road sign is wrong.
fieldNote: She trusts **written orders** and pole markers over a screen she cannot verify.
Her low wage and short savings keep **routine bills** in view despite a mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep checking switching orders against pole markers with the lead
Wait to replace appliances until one stops working

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office might send the crew a better order and reduce time spent calling around. I would still want the lead to read the live switching instructions aloud before anyone touches a line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A picture of a pole isn't the pole under the wind. I'd tell the crew we need the person on site to check the wire, the ground, and the barriers before a lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry that experienced workers will get the first callouts while juniors get shorter weeks. I don't have much practice yet, and there are few other utilities nearby where I could replace those hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my current roster and ask our worker representative to explain how dispatch decides which crew gets a job. I would write down my callout hours each month and ask for paid practical instruction when the company changes its orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because fewer shifts could mean falling behind on the mortgage. I'm not quick to trust new tools, so I'd rather see the experienced crew use them safely before I change my routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the worker representative to ask management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a rule that someone explains a roster cut and checks whether the junior crew is still getting supervised practice. I don't expect a promise of the same hours, but I want to know how a decision was made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new planning screen yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the lead shows me what it changes and how to go back to the written order. I have never used AI tools, and I wouldn't let a screen overrule the actual switching instructions.

I want the crew to check **wire, ground and barriers** before a lift.
think: I worry that junior workers will get **shorter weeks**.
I have few nearby utilities where I could replace **lost hours**.
do: Keep my current **roster** and track callout hours each month.
Ask the worker representative for **paid instruction** when orders change.
feel: I'm **anxious** about fewer shifts and cautious about unproven screens.
S1.quote: A picture of a pole isn't the pole under the wind.
fieldNote: She prefers a written instruction until the crew lead **explains a screen**.
She wants a reason for roster cuts and supervised practice for **junior workers**.

steps.text: Keep the current roster and record monthly callout hours
Ask the worker representative for review of junior roster cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years gives the company very little time to change its records and dispatch. I would expect the pole work to remain for a while, but I would not know whether the utility kept the same number of crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need the name of the person who signs off before anyone leaves the ground. A schedule from a machine does not tell me that the line has been isolated or the crew has the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have field work until robots arrive around 2031, but that's not a guarantee the company keeps me through then. I have little savings and few local alternatives, so a cut in shifts would reach my family quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the worker representative for written notice and paid training before any junior crew is removed. In 2028 I would not try to move into records or dispatch as a safe job, because AGI can do those thinking tasks. In 2029, if I'm still working, I'd take the in-person cable-rescue course the utility offers and keep earning on field shifts while they're available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because my mortgage doesn't wait for a replacement job. Three years before robots sounds like time, but it may not be enough to build savings or find another crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner when you got home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hani that we should keep the old boiler another winter and avoid a new payment until my work is clearer. We would still pay for the children's school trips, but put home decorating on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the cable-rescue course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to practise it in person with a qualified instructor and get paid for the hours. I don't want to rely on an online certificate when I have to handle a real rescue on a wet pole.

say: I need a **named person** to sign off before anyone leaves the ground.
I would ask for **notice and paid training** before junior crews are removed.
think: I may have field shifts until **2031**, but no one guarantees my job until then.
I won't treat **records or dispatch** as safe work after AGI.
do: Ask the worker representative for **written notice** before crew cuts.
Take the utility's in-person **cable-rescue course** in 2029 if still employed.
Protect the mortgage and children's **school routines** before replacing household goods.
feel: I'm **anxious** because a mortgage does not wait for another job.
S2.quote: I need the name of the person who signs off before anyone leaves the ground.
fieldNote: She wants a human to confirm **isolation and authorization** before a crew climbs.
Her training plan is in person because she does not trust **online-only instruction**.
She protects **school trips** while postponing household upgrades.

steps.text: Ask the worker representative to secure notice before junior crew cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to finish more supervised work and ask for a proper training schedule. The desk work changes in 2031, and the crews have about three more years before robots reach the physical tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that extra years help only if the training has paid hours attached. A paper promise won't help me if I have to choose between missing a shift and learning a new task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when AGI arrives and 51 when the robots do. I have time to get more competent at the job, but I'm still junior and the utility may need fewer field crews by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the crew lead for a signed list of practical tasks I need to learn and ask when the utility pays for the rescue qualification. In 2032, the first year after AGI, I'd keep taking field shifts, complete the in-person course if it is still offered, and wait for the company to publish its staffing plan before I decide about a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because three years of robot warning still leaves little room if my job ends. Five years is better than two, but my savings are too small for me to spend months waiting without pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see on the signed list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want each task to have a practice date, a qualified person to watch me, and a record I can show another utility. I don't want to move for a course that doesn't count outside this depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start applying to another utility as soon as AGI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would first wait for our actual roster and the paid course dates. If the company cuts field hours, then I would look at posted openings and compare the wages before taking my family somewhere else.

fieldNote: She wants supervised **hands-on training** that another utility will recognize.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me time to qualify for more field tasks and ask what the utility expects its crew to look like. It doesn't mean the work is safe forever, since robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the utility should show the roster and pay path several years before it changes. I won't tell my children their mother's linework will still be there when they are grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when the robots do. The longer warning gives me more time to build experience, but planning and records aren't a fallback once AGI can do thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the paper record of my practical qualifications and ask when paid rescue training is scheduled. In 2037, if I still have shifts, I'd wait for the actual roster and wages before making a decision about our youngest child's apprenticeship commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about today's mortgage and the unknown future of field work. The decade helps me plan, but my savings are still too small to make a long break from wages easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What decision about your youngest child's apprenticeship would be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2037 our youngest will be 18 and the older one will be 25. Hani and I would check whether the apprenticeship is local before promising to cover a room near a distant training site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you decide whether to stay with the utility after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to see an actual shift roster, the wage for any practical role, and the dates of paid training. I would not assume a desk transfer or an open vacancy will protect our income through the robot date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my savings are short and robots may arrive around 2031. Paid in-person training and clear notice about junior shifts would help me plan around the mortgage instead of guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I won't say yes to a new job until I know where the training and pay lead. I would want the company to show a real schedule and let workers ask how a qualification will be used.

headlineQuote: I won't say yes to a new job until I know where the training and pay lead.
portrait: Priya is a **43-year-old junior** lineworker with a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She prefers paper instructions and avoids **new technology** until she can verify it herself.
Her **thin savings** and few nearby employers make lost shifts a serious household risk.
She wants paid in-person training and **actual rosters** before moving her family or making plans.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries her most because robots may arrive around 2031 before she can build a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **in-person training** and clear notice about junior shifts would help her plan around the mortgage.
